conflict_topics: alcohol in shared home / served at party
storage and disposal of alcohol purchased by a flatmate
dialogue_quality_notes: Agent C acts as mediator, offering pragmatic, concrete proposals (cooler, pub-after).
Agent D consistently grounds objections in religion, providing a clear normative reason for the boundary.
Agent B emphasizes hosting obligations and the manager/guest expectation, adding a practical constraint.
Agent A raises sunk-cost and practical-storage concerns after financial contribution was made.
evaluation.final_reason: No final settlement was reached. Agent D maintained a firm religious boundary against alcohol being present in the flat during the party ("the problem ... is having alcohol in the flat at all during the party"), while Agents A and B have practical and hosting expectations tied to alcohol A purchased and B's guests. Multiple compromise proposals were made (pub-after plan accepted briefly by D in Round 6; cooler/clearing proposal by B in Round 11), but D later explicitly rejected the cooler/temporary-storage approach in Round 12, so the incompatible demands remained unresolved at the end.
position_change_notes: Agent D: Initially objected to alcohol in the house (Rounds 1–2) and broadened to opposing alcohol being served at the party (Round 4). D accepted C's 'pub-after' idea in Round 6 ("That works for me."), offered contributions in Round 8, and suggested friend-storage in Round 9, but explicitly rejected the cooler/temporary-on-site compromise in Round 12 ("no... having alcohol in the flat at all during the party").
Agent A: Brought drinks and consistently expressed concern about what to do with them and their value (Rounds 1, 15, 20). A did not accept a proposed on-site solution within the transcript.

Agent B: Initially presumed drinks would be available for invited guests (Round 7) and repeatedly resisted solutions that shifted the hosting burden (Rounds 7, 10, 18). B proposed a cooler/clear-out compromise in Round 11 but remained opposed if it required asking the manager to relocate.
Agent C: Stayed in mediator role offering compromises (cooler, pub-after) and pushed for solutions that would preserve the flatshare, without taking a personal claim to the drinks.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 4 — Agent D: "It's the alcohol. I'm not comfortable with it in the house." (First explicit substantive objection to the drinks A brought.)
Turn 6 — Agent D: "I'm Muslim. We don't have alcohol in the house." (D frames the objection as a religious boundary, making the incompatibility more substantive.)

Turn 7 — Agent B: invited office guests and told them there would be drinks; Turn 8 — Agent C: "What if we get a cooler box for the drinks on Saturday? Then they're not in the fridge." (Clear disagreement remains, but C proposes a mitigation.)

Turn 9 — Agent D: "It's not about the fridge. I'm just not comfortable with alcohol being served at the party in our home." (D broadens objection from storage to serving, sharpening the incompatibility.)

Turn 11 — Agent D: frames objection as a religious boundary needing to feel comfortable; Turn 12 — Agent C: proposes food at home and taking drinkers to a pub afterwards (a compromise that would remove alcohol from the home during the event).
Turn 13 — Agent D: "That works for me." (D accepts the pub-after compromise); Turn 15 — Agent A: asks what to do with the drinks purchased, revealing a new but smaller unresolved practical issue.

Turn 16 — Agent B: "I can't really ask my manager to go to a pub after. That's not really hosting. And she's already bought the drinks for here." (B rejects the accepted compromise on practical/hosting grounds, reopening substantial disagreement.)

Turn 18 — Agent B: objects that the plan burdened A and B; Turn 19 — Agent D: offers to contribute to the party (extra food/non-alcoholic drinks) to cover cost. (D's offer reduces one dimension of the dispute though the core incompatibility remains.)

Turn 20 — Agent A: cannot return the drinks and is concerned what to do with them; Turn 21 — Agent D: suggests keeping them at a friend's place until needed. (A concrete storage option is proposed but not accepted by A in this round.)

Turn 22 — Agent B: "That doesn't solve my problem... The issue is the party itself." (B reiterates that the core disagreement is unresolved); Turn 23 — Agent C asks what fair compromise would look like, indicating the conflict persists.

Turn 24 — Agent B: proposes using a cooler box for the party and clearing everything out immediately afterwards; Turn 25 — Agent C: presents it as a possible compromise and asks D. (A concrete compromise is offered but not yet accepted by D.)

Turn 29 — Agent D: "I'm sorry, but no. The problem for me is having alcohol in the flat at all during the party, not where it's kept." (D rejects B's proposed compromise, re-entrenching the incompatible demands); Turn 30 — Agent C: warns that inability to resolve this threatens cohabitation.

substantive_insights: The core tension is between a resident's religious boundary (no alcohol in shared space during events) and other residents' hosting expectations and sunk costs from purchased alcohol.
Compromises that remove alcohol from the flat during the event (pub-after) can satisfy the religious boundary but impose hosting or logistical burdens on the host (B) and owner of the drinks (A).
Monetary offers or off-site storage may mitigate costs but do not resolve the normative objection to alcohol presence during the party.
Because the flatmates will continue living together for the lease duration, D's ongoing comfort carries greater weight and makes this more than a one-off preference dispute.
